title: Design a metrics and monitoring system (like Prometheus/Grafana).
description: Time-series at scale: scrape vs push, downsampling, retention tiers, alerting semantics, and label cardinality discipline.

data.text: **Question:** Design a metrics and monitoring system that collects, stores, and alerts on time-series data from thousands of machines.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Ingest metrics (counters, gauges, histograms) from thousands of agents/services
Query recent data fast (dashboards) and historical data (capacity analysis)
Alerting with correct semantics: pending vs firing, no flapping
Retention: seconds-level for days, downsampled for months/years
High availability: no single point of failure in the monitoring path itself

data.caption: Pull-based collection with federated storage tiers and an out-of-band alerting path
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[App instances - /metrics] -->|scrape| B[Prometheus/Collector shards]
    C[Push gateway - batch jobs] --> B
    B --> D[(Time-series DB - hot)]
    D -->|downsample| E[(Long-term store - cheap)]
    D --> F[Query engine / Grafana]
    E --> F
    B -->|remote-write| G[Alert Manager]
    G --> H[PagerDuty/Email/Slack]
    I[Blackbox probes - synthetic] --> B

data.text: The defining choice is **pull vs push**: Prometheus-style **pull** (scrape /metrics from each target) gives service discovery, health inference (target down = scrape failing), and simple fan-in; **push** (agents/remote-write) suits short-lived jobs, serverless, and cross-network boundaries. Most production systems mix both, funneling into a **time-series database** with hot/cold tiers and an **alert manager** kept out-of-band so monitoring survives what it monitors.

items: Data model: (metric name, label set, timestamp, value) — labels enable slicing (region, host, endpoint); every label multiplies series count
Cardinality discipline is THE scaling lever: endpoint labels must be low-cardinality routes (/orders/{id} as /orders), never raw URLs/user ids
Storage: append-only time-series chunks (compressed columns), sorted by series; hot tier in memory+SSD (days), cold tier object-storage-backed with coarse resolution (months)
Downsampling: raw 15s for ~2 weeks, 5m for months, 1h for years — dashboards over a year read pre-aggregated data, not raw points
Histograms over averages: latency histograms (bucket counts) let you compute p95/p99 correctly at query time — averages hide the tail

Alerting semantics: rule evaluates over the query (e.g., error_rate > 5% for 10m) → PENDING → FIRING after 'for' duration; grouping, inhibition (don't page for node-down AND pod-down), and silences live in the alert manager
HA: scrape shards by target hash, each TSDB replicated; alerting evaluates from replicated data with rules deduped (one alertmanager cluster, leader-based)
Federation/global view: regional Prometheus + central remote-write/store for cross-region dashboards; alert locally so regional failures still page
The monitoring of the monitoring: blackbox probes (synthetic transactions), TSDB health, alert-pipeline tests — the observability stack crashing silently is the worst failure mode

data.title: Labels are a schema — treat them like one
data.text: A single unbounded label (user_id, raw URL) turns 50k series into 50 million and melts every node in the cluster. Enforce label allow-lists at the agent/collector, use recording rules for expensive aggregations, and review new metrics like you review DB indexes: they're a shared, finite resource.

rows: One time stream; identity = name + labels

items: Scrape target flapping — up/down churn creates alert noise; use 'for' durations and up{}-based meta-alerts
Clock skew between agents — normalize at ingest; out-of-order samples need late-acceptance windows
Cardinality explosion from a deploy (new label value) — ingest-side limits and metric quarantine
Alert storm during an incident — inhibition rules (parent alerts silence children)
TSDB compaction racing queries — snapshot-aware compaction or query-time chunk stitching
Short-lived batch jobs — push gateway or push metrics with explicit job lifetime, else they vanish between scrapes

items.question: Pull or push — which is better?
items.answer: Pull (Prometheus) wins for long-running services: discovery, health, and no agent needed beyond an endpoint. Push (agents, remote-write, OpenTelemetry collector) wins for ephemeral workloads and network boundaries. Most stacks converge on a collector doing both.

items.question: How do you alert without drowning in pages?
items.answer: Page on user-visible symptoms (SLI burn-rate alerts, like the multi-window error-budget approach) rather than on every internal metric; ticket on causes; 'for' durations for state, fast only for catastrophic signals.

items.question: Where does OpenTelemetry fit?
items.answer: OTel is the instrumentation/transport standard: apps emit via OTel SDK → collector → TSDB/backends. It decouples what you instrument from where metrics/logs/traces go, replacing per-vendor agents.

items.question: How do you capacity-plan the monitoring system itself?
items.answer: Series count × sample rate × bytes/sample is the cost model; cardinality audits, scrape-interval tuning, and downsampling are the levers. Always headroom for incident-time spikes, when you need it most.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Time-series DB: append-only chunks, hot/cold tiers, downsampling for long retention
Label cardinality is the scaling dial — enforce it at ingest
Histograms for percentiles; alert on SLI burn, with for-durations and inhibition
Keep the monitoring path itself monitored (blackbox probes, HA scrape/alert)
data.takeaway: A monitoring system is a database with a pager attached — design the schema (labels) conservatively, tier the storage, and page on symptoms people feel.
